 Rains may prolong dengue outbreak into Dec
 Experts call for targeted mosquito-control measures 
 Published : 21 November 2026
 • 
 Updated : 21 November 2026, 09:47
 • 
 DISEASE
 SHARE 
 Helemul Alam
 Helemul Alam 
 The ongoing rainfall in November could prolong Bangladesh’s dengue outbreak into December , as Aedes mosquito populations may not decline as expected, experts have warned. 
 According to the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), the country is likely to experience persistent rain or thundershowers accompanied by temporary gusty winds from November 19 to 23 under the influence of cyclone “Akvan”.
 Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source 
 Entomologist Prof Kabirul Bashar said dengue cases usually decline significantly in December, but the rainfall could create new breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes, prolonging the outbreak.
 He said the situation could become more challenging as Culex mosquito populations may also increase, worsening mosquito nuisance in urban areas.
 Read more No respite from dengue as winter approaches 
 He stressed the need for regular removal of breeding sources and appropriate use of larvicides to control both species.
 Entomologist Manjur A Chowdhury said rainfall, higher-than-expected temperatures and increased humidity could favour Aedes breeding and extend dengue transmission into December.
 “The season has already been prolonged, and it may continue further,” he said, warning that dengue cases and deaths could remain significant throughout December.
 However, Dr Manjur said temperatures and humidity might decline by the time newly hatched mosquitoes mature in seven to 10 days, limiting the immediate impact on transmission.
 He said the dengue death toll had already crossed 500 this year, potentially making it one of the deadliest outbreaks in recent years.
 Actual infections could be several times higher than official figures, as many patients do not seek hospital care or receive treatment outside the surveillance system, he added.
 Dr Manjur advised people to use mosquito nets, apply aerosol insecticides in the morning and evening, wear long-sleeved clothing and remove stagnant water from homes and surrounding areas weekly.
 He also urged vigilance in households with dengue patients to prevent mosquitoes from spreading the virus to others.
 Read more Dengue threat unlikely to ease before December 
 Calling for community-level mosquito control, he identified construction sites, vacant plots, unmanaged garbage and abandoned containers as potential breeding grounds, particularly in Bashundhara, Badda and Banasree.
 He urged authorities to conduct targeted mosquito-control operations based on disease surveillance rather than relying mainly on awareness campaigns and routine measures.
 Early identification of dengue-positive households and surrounding areas could help contain local clusters, he said.
 Dr Manjur also called for stronger surveillance to assess infections outside Dhaka and for dengue to be declared a notifiable disease.
